title: The star formation region NGC 3324
caption: The star formation region NGC 3324, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla
celestial: NGC 3324 · constellation Carina · about 7500 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This view, taken with the Wide Field Imager camera mounted on La Silla's 2.2-meter MPG/ESO telescope, shows NGC 3324, a region where stars are forming.

NGC 3324 is home to several massive, blue-white stars, and their influence is written into the shape of the nebula. Their intense radiation has hollowed out a space in the gas and dust around them, pushing material away and leaving a clearing around them. Star-forming regions commonly follow this pattern. Once big, hot stars are born, they begin to reshape and eventually disperse the cloud that made them.

The same stars are also responsible for the colors. Their ultraviolet radiation makes the gas cloud glow in rich hues, as atoms energized by that light release it again at particular wavelengths. The telescope recorded the scene through broad filters and narrow ones tuned to the glow of oxygen and hydrogen, which help pick out where different gases are shining. The official caption offers few further details.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (26.43 x 26.43 arcminutes) and distance (7500 light years), the frame spans roughly 58 × 58 light-years. Its light set out about 7,500 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This visible-light image from the Wide Field Imager combines V and R filters with narrow filters for oxygen and hydrogen light. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Long exposures gather far more light than the eye, so the glowing gas looks far richer in color than it would through an eyepiece.
